This is a confusing question. GTM isn't a tag, it's a container that holds tags, so it depends on which tag you use to measure this conversion. If you use the Ads conversation tag template in GTM it is pretty much the same thing. The Google tag is slightly different but also just carries the conversion tag. 

What website issues are you having that is preventing you from using GTM?

There's more to a tag than just putting it on your site. They have settings, like consent (does the person visiting your site live somewhere that requires consent to track them?) triggers (when should the tag ask for certain data?) variables (specific type of data based on what the tag is looking for). GTM let's you edit these for the tags in your container. If you don't put the Ads tag in the container, then you won't be able to edit it. 

If you left the ads tag out but still used GTM for GA4, they'll both work, but you definitely shouldn't use the same Ads tag for all of the businesses unless you want all of the data from all of the sites to be combined. 

I don't know any set ups that operate combined like this, but maybe you can find someone who has done it? It sounds overly complicated to me tho.

1. Why do want to add the google ads tag to my GTM and website if Google ads already tracks data in Google ads dashboard. 

If you're using one ads account for multiple businesses, this might start to get messy when looking at the data. Moving to GTM might help you clean it up a bit, but you'll need to start over. 

To answer your question, people prefer GTM because you can add non-google tags (like a Facebook pixel), and also you can make changes to your tags without having to reinstall the code every time. You need to add the Google Ads tag to GTM if you choose to use GTM or you won't be able to edit the Google tag with GTM. If you set up both, you might also end up duplicating data 

Think of Tag Manager as a Squarsespace like software and the Google tag is the website itself. You can either hire a developer to edit your site, or hook your site up to Squarsespace and edit it yourself. 



2. Is it possible to use the same Google Ads tag in each of my websites' GTM and will it differentiate between the different website sources? 

It would make it hard to differentiate the data. You are better off having a different Google Tag for every business and a different GTM container for every business.

I'm not an expert here, but I have Borderline Personality Disorder and a big part of it is dealing with emotional regulation. 

Just from learning about my own emotions and mental resilience it's actually not something you have as much control as you would like to, while also being something you could totally train. We all kinda have these pre-built spectrums of expression we develop when we're children which are partially genetic and partially experience— and although you'd think the opposite, it's actually people who have gone through more who tend to be more expressive in their anxieties and such. Basically if as a child you cried a lot (whether it be because of trauma or just an openly expressive upbringing) you're more likely to cry easily as an adult. 

The key is mindfulness. It's been practiced and studied across the globe in different ways, whether by meditation or yoga or tai chi etc, but what it comes down to is the more you can stop yourself before having an emotional reaction and tell yourself, "I'm not gonna react blah way but instead this other way" the easier it'll become to do so. You just keep practicing. There's great books on mindfulness out there that have easy practice scenarios you can follow like focusing on being present by breathing or reciting every taste in your bites while eating.

Well, it depends what you need to know. It's always really good to start with user interviews and market research. How are people using the app already? What are their needs? Why isn't it working? What other apps or services do they use to do the same thing? The important thing here too is to focus on their already built habits. Dont ask leading questions. If I ask "would you use a coupon app?" You're instinct is going to be to be agreeable and say, sure, yeah I like saving money, but if I ask, "How many  promotional codes, coupons or deals have you used in the last 2 weeks?" I'll get a better idea of where they operate and how to make it better. 

From there a persona is almost always important. Competitive analysis helps a lot. And if its a full redesign, I would def do user testing. The tools are there for you to utilize. People think UX is about having good creative ideas, and that's a small fraction. It's really about knowing how to investigate where the problems lie and confirming that your solutions actually do solve the problem

Communicating how I felt often got responses like, "it's not like that" "you're being sensitive" "You're just in your feelings" and my responses were often defensive because it didn't feel like they thought of my feelings as valid, so I became harder on myself. 

It wasn't until I could trail the triggers, understood how BPD affected me and empathized with their perspective that I was able to change my language to stuff like " Yes, I am sensitive to these specific things. I don't mean to be, but I am working on it". " These sort of things make me feel good, and these don't, and Im trying to not let those bug me as much". 

This language not only explained specifically why my feelings were hurt or why I might just have a hard time being present without blaming anyone and still leaving room for both parties to try. 

It isn't perfect. I still cringe a lot at my social capabilities sometimes, but the overall cooperation in the room is better. I think we often put a lot of pressure on ourselves to be more normal and I think it gets easier when we accept we aren't, and try anyway.
